articles.sourceTitle: Frontier AI labs say their models refuted the Exponential Time Hypothesis. What does that mean?
articles.title: Frontier AI labs say their models refuted the Exponential Time Hypothesis. What does that mean?
articles.text:
OpenAI released solutions to three blockbuster math problems that have long vexed researchers yesterday. One was a surprise rejection of the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), a durable assumption in computer science that plays a large role in how we understand what is difficult to compute.

As with previous proof-drops from the frontier lab, scientific communities responded with a mixture of thrill and dismay. Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge suggested that OpenAI was basing its solutions from pre-existing work, and hours later, Anthropic subsequently released its own refutation of ETH.

However, OpenAI’s process is evolving. This time, the lab structured its releases differently for each of the three disciplines involved: Mathematicians got the work dropped on GitHub; the computer scientists formed a working group, asked for the proofs to be shared publicly and OpenAI to fund a conference to discuss them; the physicists formed a working group that will determine how their result will be released.

MIT Professor Ryan Williams is the computer scientist who is organizing his field’s response to the new finding. Williams, whose work focuses on these questions of computational complexity, has criticized OpenAI’s approach in the past, calling its proof dump earlier this October a “DDOS attack on mathematicians.”

However, he agreed to collaborate with the frontier labs in order to help shepherd ideas that are vital to the field, he told TechCrunch. The lab asked him to help interpret the solution, along with UC San Diego computer scientists Russell Impagliazzo and Ramamohan Paturi, who first published the ETH in 1999.

Their first step was to release an open letter calling for feedback from scientists interested in these problems and a discussion of the norms around AI contributions to their work.

“Some parts [of OpenAI’s proof] are, maybe you could say routine, but then yes, there are two or three alien-looking parts, and it’s exactly these parts that that I saw that made me think, wow, this is something that the whole community needs to work on together,” Williams told TechCrunch.

Are you down with P vs NP?

The ETH is part of a broader class of problems known as P vs NP, which has animated computer science and many other fields for decades. Reductively, researchers are trying to understand if any problem whose solution can be easily verified (NP) can also be easily solved (P).

A simple example is the game Sodoku: Once a solution to a puzzle is in place, it can be quickly verified, but finding the solution is time-consuming. That dynamic is true across a range of important problems, and the insight underpins cryptographic systems: When you have the key to an encoded message, you can reveal it, but actually cracking an effective code takes too long to be useful.

However, scientists have yet to prove whether that is always true. “P = NP is saying that, not only can you verify Sudoku solutions when they exist, you can just generate them,” Williams said. “P = NP is asserting that this is true for every single problem you can verify quickly — if you can verify it quickly, you can solve it quickly. So this just seems that just seems too good to be true.”

That’s why most scientists assume that P ≠ NP. ETH provided evidence for that. It basically says that even the fastest computer algorithm needs exponentially more time to find a solution as the number of variables grow in a specific class of tricky logic puzzle.

The claims from OpenAI and Anthropic is that their models have come up with algorithms that solve those puzzles in “sub-exponential” time, meaning faster than the speeds previously thought possible. If true, they may have proven the EFT to be false — refuted it, in scientific terms — and maybe opened up a path for algorithms that generally perform P = NP.

“Every computer scientist should probably put a a little more weight on the plausibility of P = NP, but one’s weight may vary,” Williams said. “I do think that it kind of calls into question a lot of the intuitions that we thought we had about … how tractable [hard NP problems] are. I also think that this is probably not the final answer either. I don’t think that OpenAI’s algorithm could possibly be the best algorithm you can get.”

The work ahead for computer scientists

The durability of ETH has lead to it being included in many scientific papers over the past decade that will need to be revisited if the AI labs claims that they’ve proven it wrong holds up, Williams said.

“This is partly why I was asking or pushing OpenAI to support a conference on this — it’s going to affect many researchers’ works, and we need to figure out, okay, what happens next besides understanding the algorithms, we need to understand, what should the foundations be that we had before?” he said.Before scientific concerns, there are cybersecurity questions. Williams said that an improved algorithm could imply that cryptographic systems relying on certain key sizes could be considered broken. So one of the first questions he asked OpenAI science lead Dan Roberts “was if they had checked that that this affects any crypto systems … is anything insecure now? And apparently, they checked, and they were reasonably confident that this didn’t … imply any breaks.”

This new AI paradigm of scientific discovery is still a work in progress, but Williams says he is optimistic despite real concerns, particularly about training the next generation of scientists. Being a computer scientist who does high level math has perhaps made the adjustment easier for him than for pure mathematicians.

Still, he says AI is “forcing people to be a little more ambitious about the kind of work that they do, and to think more deeply about okay, if all the things I used to work on are now low hanging fruit for AI, how can I raise the bar for the the kind of scientific questions I want to ask?”

articles.sourceTitle: AI promised less work. I've never worked more
articles.title: AI Promised Less Work. I Have Never Worked More.
articles.text:
The pitch was that AI would give us our time back. Write less boilerplate, delegate the boring parts, go home earlier.
I am not complaining about the tools. I use agents for all of my engineering work now, and I wrote about how that setup evolved and why I still read the code. I can investigate and ship things that would not have been worth starting two years ago.
But somewhere this year I noticed that I am working more than I ever have, and that it feels heavier than it used to. Not because any single task is harder. Because there are so many more of them, all at once.
This post is me trying to understand that, with some data from my own GitHub history.
The old load and the new load
As a full-stack engineer, a normal week for me meant two or three serious tasks. A feature, a tricky bug, maybe a migration. Each one needed real focus, but I could hold one of them in my head at a time, finish it, and move to the next.
Today my week looks completely different. I have several agents running in parallel: one implementing a change, one investigating a production question, one working through a review, another doing research I will need later. None of them needs me all the time. Every one of them needs me sometimes.
That “sometimes” is the problem.
Each agent eventually comes back with a question, a plan to approve, a diff to read or a result to make sense of. Responding means switching contexts: reloading a different problem, a different repository and a different set of decisions.
Two or three serious tasks a week was tiring in a familiar way. Working with many agents is tiring in a new way. My attention is spread across more problems, and I find moving between them much more mentally draining.
What my GitHub history shows
I pulled my GitHub contribution calendar for every month from January 2019 to today and marked my roles at Bold.org, which I joined in January 2020: Full Stack Engineer until August 2022, Principal Engineer until August 2025, and Vice President of Technology since then. These are GitHub’s contribution counts, including private work, so they mix commits, pull requests, reviews and issues. It is a rough signal of activity, not a measure of value. 2019 is an incomplete baseline: my job before Bold.org used a self-hosted GitLab, so GitHub only shows what I did outside it. But the shape is hard to ignore.

The first part of the curve is what I expected:

My busiest coding years at Bold.org were the early ones. 2020 was my highest year, with 2,711 contributions. 2021 dropped to 1,839 and 2022 to 1,498.
The Principal Engineer years were flat and lower. From August 2022 to July 2025 I averaged 114 contributions a month, against 173 as a Full Stack Engineer. My lowest year was 2023, with 1,189.
The first months as VP of Technology looked the same. From August to December 2025 I averaged 111 a month, and December 2025 was my quietest month since joining Bold.org, with 50.

As a Principal Engineer, more of my work went into architecture, deep dives into concepts, setting up projects and planning, rather than fixing bugs or iterating on features. Becoming VP of Technology continued that shift, with even less feature work expected. At least until AI came along.
Then 2026 happened:

I am back at my Full Stack Engineer pace. By October 27 I am at 2,102 contributions, already more than any full year from 2021 to 2025. Over the same period in 2020 I had 2,371, so 2026 is close to my busiest year but not above it.
August 2026 is the busiest month in the whole timeline. 427 contributions, against a previous high of 319 in April 2020.
My normal day moved back up. The median weekday was 3 or 4 contributions every year from 2022 to 2025. In 2026 it is 7, close to the 8 I had in 2020.
Fewer weekdays without GitHub activity. Through October 27, I had 18 weekdays with zero contributions, compared with 40–46 across each full year from 2022 to 2025. These are days without recorded GitHub activity, not days off work.
Heavy days became routine again. From 2022 to 2025 I had exactly one day per year with 24 or more contributions. In 2026 I already have 16, almost the 17 I had in all of 2020.

Almost all of this is private work. The dashed line in the chart is public contributions only: it was near zero from 2021 to 2025 and came back this year, with 191 so far, but that is still less than a tenth of 2026.
The twist is the role. In 2020 I was a full-stack engineer doing feature work full time, and this is roughly what that looked like on GitHub. Today I lead engineering at Bold.org and do far less feature work than I used to. On paper my graph should look like my Principal Engineer years, or lower. Instead it is back where it was when writing code was my whole job.
What changed is how much work feels worth taking on. When coding is cheap, I can fix bugs I would previously have left alone, improve patterns across the codebase, take on new projects and turn more ideas into something real. Much of this is work I would never have considered before. Agents did not just make my existing workload faster to finish. They made it easy to give myself a much bigger one.
Bursts, then burnout
Looking at the monthly totals, 2026 is not one steady climb. It is a series of bursts.
January and February were the first clear burst, with 277 and 233 contributions. This is when I started working seriously with agents, and when the observability experiment that became our internal company agent took off. Every week revealed something new I could suddenly delegate, and I wanted to try all of it.
March to June generally winds down, from 203 contributions in March to 77 in June. But April was a smaller burst along the way, another month when I had ideas and acted on them. I think improvements in the models were part of that renewed energy. Its monthly total of 187 is below January to March, but it includes a 29-contribution day and 68 public contributions, my highest public total of the year.
August is the biggest burst of all. Coming back from my summer break, the calendar shows a full week of zero contributions in early August. Then every weekday from August 10 to August 27 was between 14 and 43. August ended at 427 contributions, the busiest month in the whole timeline. September stayed high at 301.
Every cycle starts the same way. A new model or a new workflow makes something possible that was not possible last month, and my head fills with ideas. Because implementation is now cheap, there is no natural friction stopping me from pursuing all of them at once. So I do. I start more agents, open more threads and say yes to more experiments.
That works for a few weeks. Then the reviewing and context switching catch up with me, and I pull back to a more stable flow. I stay there until something exciting comes along, or until a holiday recharges me enough that I go straight back into another burst.
I count three of these cycles since January.
At the end of a burst, I feel tired of AI. I do not want to start another agent or think of more ideas. I do my normal work, but I stop chasing the extra projects and possibilities because I do not have the mental bandwidth for them.
The low season is not low anymore
The part that surprised me most is not the peaks. It is how much I am doing between them.
March did not feel like the bursts in January, February or August, but I was still doing substantial work. It had 203 contributions, against my Principal Engineer average of 114 a month. I was still acting on ideas, but that level of activity no longer felt like an exceptional push. Even when I think I am taking it easy, there are still agent results to work through, reviews to finish and small things that are now “just a quick prompt”.
June was genuinely low, with 77 contributions, comparable to my quieter Principal Engineer months. Maybe that was when all the tiredness caught up with me. Not every quiet month is higher than before. But outside the bursts, I still find myself taking on more work than I used to. That is what I mean by the low season not feeling low anymore.
Where that leaves me
AI made room for work I would never have considered before. I like being able to fix more things and turn more ideas into something real. But the capacity to implement those ideas has grown much faster than my capacity to think about them. Eventually I stop wanting to start another agent and go back to just doing my normal work. I have not figured out a balance. For now, I am noticing that being able to do more keeps turning into doing more. And I am tired.

A note on how this article was written: AI helped me pull and analyze my GitHub contribution data, build the chart and draft this article. The experience, decisions and opinions are mine.

articles.title: Inside Wikipedia’s Cleanup of AI-Generated Content
articles.text:
Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup, a volunteer effort launched in 2023 to find and remove AI-generated material from Wikipedia that breaks the website’s guidelines. When the cleanup began, AI writing was often betrayed by conspicuous clichés. Today, the project’s volunteers are developing tools to detect subtler forms of machine-generated content and debating AI’s role in the world’s most widely used encyclopedia. When did you realize Wikipedia had a problem with AI-generated material?Ellia Lebleu: It was around December 2023. A few other editors and I were chatting on Wikipedia’s Discord server, and we had all seen very strange articles with the same odd characteristics. They repeated phrases like “stands as a testament” or “rich cultural heritage.” They sometimes had conclusion sections, or sections called “Why is this important?” That was very typical of ChatGPT in 2023 and early 2024 but very odd for Wikipedia articles—and very easy to spot. Then I decided, let’s create an official project on Wikipedia so more people can deal with this.

Ellia Lebleu

Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup. Lebleu is pursuing a Ph.D. in AI at the Inria Center of the University of Rennes, part of France’s national research institute for digital science and technology.How do editors spot AI-generated writing today?Lebleu: By 2025, the signs of AI writing were becoming subtler and more structural. For example, AI loves the “rule of three,” negative parallelisms, and other structures of speech that aren’t conclusive by themselves but become meaningful as they accumulate. We also look beyond the article. If someone writes five articles of thousands of words each in 5 minutes, there is reason to suspect AI.Does the AI problem just appear in the main text, or also in citations?Lebleu: Fake or misleading citations have become a major worry. Sometimes an AI hallucinates a citation entirely, although that’s much rarer today because of retrieval-augmented generation that allows the AI to find sources. More often, it finds a real source but gets its content completely wrong. AI citations that don’t actually support what is being written are extremely commonplace.English Wikipedia recently prohibited editors from using LLMs to generate articles. How much AI-generated content is still getting through?Lebleu: I’ve been working with [AI-detection company] Pangram to estimate the proportion of AI-generated content. I tested it on Wikipedia content from before ChatGPT and found no false positives, so its results provide a very conservative lower bound. In late 2025, it flagged perhaps 20 percent of new articles and drafts as AI-generated. In early 2026, that went down to 15 or 16 percent. But we don’t yet know whether that’s because our recent policies have had an effect or because models are getting more powerful and Pangram hasn’t had time to adapt.Is Wikipedia using AI to combat AI?Lebleu: Another Wikipedia editor has made an AI source verifier, which goes through the sources on a page and checks whether they match the claims. Since it is itself an AI model, there is no guarantee that it will be correct every time. But if you want something that works at scale and filters out obvious cases, it’s a good first step. The Wikimedia Foundation is also working on a tool called Paste Check, which can flag text pasted directly from some AI chatbots.And we’ve seen Claude sometimes say, “I can’t write a Wikipedia article; it would go against Wikipedia’s policies.” If all major AI companies implemented that kind of prompt refusal, it wouldn’t solve the problem entirely, because there are still open-weight models that can be tweaked to avoid restrictions. But it would help with people who use commercial models and aren’t especially familiar with the technology. Can you tell if the rule prohibiting AI writing is working?Lebleu: It’s still a little early to tell. We see possible effects, such as prompt refusal and the apparent slight drop in AI-generated content. But again, we don’t yet know if that is because models are getting better or because beginners are learning the rules. The vast majority of AI-generated content is submitted by beginner editors, so we’ve made many efforts to make the rule very visible in welcome messages, editing help, and advice. What if AI becomes capable of writing truly reliable Wikipedia articles?Lebleu: That’s one of the big questions we’re facing. When the guideline was passed, it was for very practical reasons: We were flooded with AI content, we didn’t have good tools, and we needed to put a stop to it. But since then, it has taken on a more philosophical dimension. Many people have called Wikipedia “the last good place on the internet.” Being a place that was, in theory, free from AI slop has become part of Wikipedia’s identity.A lot of Wikipedia’s communication is now centered on the idea that we’re a human-written encyclopedia. Even AI companies find that interesting. It can be valuable to have a purely human-written corpus on which to [train] AI systems. The fact that Wikipedia is still that, and will remain that for at least the near future, makes it a precious resource that isn’t replicated anywhere else.But will the people who read and contribute to Wikipedia want it to become partially AI-generated if that makes it more comprehensive? We could preserve Wikipedia’s identity as a human-written corpus while also offering an AI-assisted option.Has Wikipedia reckoned with the idea of “Google Zero”—a possible future in which websites no longer get traffic from Google search?Lebleu: If everything goes through AI search and websites plummet to zero visibility, how do we expose Wikipedia and show that it can be edited and that people can still contribute? Wikipedia is frequently cited in [Google’s] AI Overviews, but users may only see an AI answer citing Wikipedia. They may not realize that Wikipedia is a living project they can edit and contribute to.The Wikimedia Foundation is working on an attribution framework that could give AI users more information about the article [being cited]: when it was last edited, how comprehensive it is, whether editors have flagged problems, and perhaps even a call to action. In the future, readers might even contribute through AI models: “The AI cited Wikipedia, but there seems to be an error. Can I make an edit request and add this other source I found?”I can see a very strong symbiotic relationship between Wikipedia and AI models in the future. I don’t see Wikipedia disappearing, but I can see it taking a very different shape. Yesterday, AI was something to clean up. Today, it’s a tool to help us with the cleanup. Tomorrow, it will be the air we breathe.A condensed version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue as “Ellia Lebleu.”

articles.sourceTitle: The Mythical Man-Month in the Age of AI
articles.title: The Mythical Man-Month in the age of AI
articles.text:
The Mythical Man-Month in the age of AI

27 October 2026

Last weekend I watched four people desperately trying to get a laptop to connect to a screen. I was happily observing their efforts, with zero intent to join in.
But someone nudged me: can't you have a look at it?
My reply: "Haha sorry no! My experience is that adding more people will not solve this problem any quicker".
I was of course -- indirectly -- referring to Brooks's Law:

"Adding manpower to a late software project makes it later."

It was formulated by computer scientist Frederick P. Brooks Jr. in his 1975 book The Mythical Man-Month, based on his experience managing the IBM OS/360 project.
However I got to thinking. Does this still hold up in the age of AI agents and LLMs?
At first glance, you’d think no. The traditional bottlenecks -- onboarding time, endless stand-ups, and office politics -- disappear overnight. An AI agent is up to speed in milliseconds and doesn't demand a coffee break.
But when you look closer, and the law hasn't vanished. It just mutated.
The famous "Baby Problem" remains: nine agents still can’t deliver a baby in one month. Sequential tasks are still sequential.
Overhead hasn't disappeared; it shifted: instead of managing people, you are now managing agents. Someone still needs to define "done", review the code, catch hallucinations, and stitch the pieces together.
That someone is you.
Throw nine autonomous agents at a single codebase without crystal-clear orchestration, and they will happily rewrite each other's work in a high-speed loop.
Maybe the 2026 update to Brooks’s Law should be:

"Adding agents to a project with unclear requirements gets you the wrong answer faster."
